title: "Central moments"

The preceding pages introduced [variance as an expected squared
distance](variance-and-covariance.qmd#variance-as-expected-squared-distance) and
[standard deviation](standard-deviation.qmd#definition) as its square root.
But the empirical CMUdict phone-count distribution is asymmetric, with a small
number of entries much farther above the mean than below it. Changing the
exponent on the centered deviation gives a family of summaries sensitive to
different aspects of that shape.

We recover variance as the second central moment, use the third and fourth moments to describe asymmetry and tail weight, and then explain why finitely many moments do not determine a distribution in general.

The [**$k$th central moment**](https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.01%3A_Definitions_and_Basic_Properties) of $X$ centers first and then raises the deviation to power $k$:

$$
\mu_k
\equiv\mathbb{E}\!\left[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^k\right],
$$

when this expectation exists. The word *central* indicates that each value is centered by subtracting the mean before the power is applied.

```{r}
#| label: load-cmudict-moments
library(ggplot2)

cmu <- read.csv(
  "data/cmudict/cmudict-pronunciations.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE,
  na.strings = ""
)
phone_pmf <- as.data.frame(table(cmu$phone_count))
names(phone_pmf) <- c("phone_count", "entries")
phone_pmf$phone_count <- as.integer(as.character(phone_pmf$phone_count))
phone_pmf$mass <- phone_pmf$entries / nrow(cmu)

phone_mean <- sum(phone_pmf$phone_count * phone_pmf$mass)
central_moment <- function(order) {
  sum((phone_pmf$phone_count - phone_mean)^order * phone_pmf$mass)
}
moment_values <- vapply(1:4, central_moment, numeric(1))
phone_sd <- sqrt(moment_values[2])
phone_skewness <- moment_values[3] / phone_sd^3
phone_kurtosis <- moment_values[4] / phone_sd^4

phone_pmf$third_moment_contribution <-
  (phone_pmf$phone_count - phone_mean)^3 * phone_pmf$mass
phone_pmf$direction <- ifelse(
  phone_pmf$phone_count < phone_mean,
  "Below mean",
  "Above mean"
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(cmu) == 133854L,
  abs(moment_values[1]) < 1e-10,
  abs(moment_values[2] -
        mean((cmu$phone_count - mean(cmu$phone_count))^2)) < 1e-12,
  all(is.finite(moment_values))
)

data.frame(
  order = 1:4,
  central_moment = moment_values
)
```

## The first and second central moments

For $k=1$,

$$
\mu_1
=\mathbb{E}[X-\mathbb{E}[X]]
=0.
$$

The computed first central moment is `r format(moment_values[1], scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)`, which differs from zero only through floating-point arithmetic.

For $k=2$,

$$
\mu_2
=\mathbb{E}\!\left[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2\right]
=\operatorname{Var}[X].
$$

The empirical second central moment is `r sprintf("%.3f", moment_values[2])` phones squared, and its square root is the standard deviation reported on the preceding page.

## The third central moment

For $k=3$, the sign of each centered value remains. The empirical third central moment is `r sprintf("%.3f", moment_values[3])` phones cubed. Its positive sign reflects the greater cubed contribution of counts above the mean.

```{r}
#| label: plot-cmudict-third-moment
#| fig-cap: "Contribution of each observed phone count to the third central moment. Color only distinguishes direction relative to the empirical mean."
ggplot(phone_pmf,
       aes(phone_count, third_moment_contribution, fill = direction)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Below mean" = "grey", "Above mean" = "steelblue"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(x = "Phones in pronunciation",
       y = "Contribution to third central moment") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

A standardized third central moment divides by $\sigma_X^3$ so that the units cancel:

$$
\frac{\mu_3}{\sigma_X^3}.
$$

This unitless summary is often called skewness. Its empirical value is `r sprintf("%.3f", phone_skewness)`.

Standardization is what permits comparison across measurement scales: if
phone counts were rescaled, both $\mu_3$ and $\sigma^3$ would change by the
same factor. Their ratio is unitless.

## The fourth central moment

The fourth central moment is

$$
\mu_4
=\mathbb{E}\!\left[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^4\right].
$$

Dividing $\mu_4$ by $\sigma_X^4$ gives a unitless summary often called kurtosis:

$$
\frac{\mu_4}{\sigma_X^4}.
$$

The empirical fourth central moment is `r sprintf("%.3f", moment_values[4])` phones to the fourth power, and the standardized value is `r sprintf("%.3f", phone_kurtosis)`. This summary is sensitive to probability far from the mean, but one value does not reveal where that probability lies.

Some sources report **excess kurtosis**, defined as
$\mu_4/\sigma^4-3$, so that a normal distribution has value zero. This page
reports kurtosis itself, not excess kurtosis. Stating the convention prevents a
three-unit discrepancy from becoming a substantive disagreement.

## A moment does not determine a distribution

An even power makes departures on both sides positive, while an odd power preserves direction. Increasing the power gives progressively more weight to values far from the mean. But a central moment does not provide a complete account of distribution shape, and different distributions can share the same first several moments.

For instance, a variable equally likely to be $-1$ or $1$ and a variable with
masses $1/4,1/2,1/4$ at $-\sqrt2,0,\sqrt2$ both have mean zero and variance one.
The first is two-point and the second is three-point; their fourth moments are
one and two. Matching center and spread thus does not match shape.

Plots locate which values create a summary. That is why the empirical contribution plot accompanies the algebra.

## Check your understanding

1. Recompute the first four central moments for `phone_count`.
2. Why is the first central moment zero whenever the mean exists?
3. Why do odd central moments retain direction while even moments do not?
4. Remove the pronunciation entries at the observed maximum `phone_count` and recompute skewness. Which tail contribution changed?
5. If software reports excess kurtosis, how should the page's standardized
   fourth moment be converted?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. For total `phone_count`, the first four empirical central moments are approximately $0$, $4.566130$, $7.452172$, and $85.066716$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The first central moment is zero because $\mathbb{E}[X-\mathbb{E}[X]]=\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[X]=0$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Odd powers preserve the sign of a centered deviation, whereas even powers make deviations on both sides nonnegative. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Removing the single 32-phone entry reduces skewness from $0.763766$ to $0.752368$ by removing an extreme upper-tail contribution. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. Subtract 3 from $\mu_4/\sigma^4$; conversely, add 3 to convert excess
   kurtosis back to the convention used here.

</details>

Central moments vary the power applied to deviations from the mean, and
standardization removes the units from moments three and four. These summaries
remain partial: no short list of moments determines distributional shape in
general. The [next page](bernoulli-and-categorical-distributions.qmd) begins the
distribution-family pages using these shared summaries.
